fields.name: Probability and Statistics Foundations
fields.description: Probability and statistics give the vocabulary for every later model. This week covers conditioning, inference, limit theorems, return distributions, and simulation, and each idea is checked against simulated data.

fields.name: Time Series and Stochastic Processes
fields.description: Financial data is ordered in time, so models must respect that order. This week covers stationarity, ARIMA models, volatility models, random-walk price dynamics, and mean reversion between related series.

fields.name: Linear Algebra and Numerical Python
fields.description: Portfolio mathematics, regression and most machine learning models reduce to matrix operations. This week covers matrix algebra, factorizations, covariance estimation, and writing that math as fast vectorized code.

fields.name: FIX Protocol and Trading Connectivity
fields.description: FIX is the standard messaging language between buy-side firms, brokers and exchanges. This week covers the wire format, session rules, the order lifecycle, Python tooling, and how to test a connection safely.

fields.name: Market Microstructure and Order Management
fields.description: Microstructure explains how prices form from orders, and an order management system controls how orders reach the market. This week covers order books, order types, impact and costs, order management, and pre-trade risk controls.

fields.name: Fixed Income and Derivatives Pricing
fields.description: Fixed income is a set of cash flows discounted along a yield curve, and most pricing models build on that idea. This week covers bond pricing, duration, curve construction, swaps, and option pricing, with checks against market-standard libraries.

fields.name: Futures, Forex and Market Data Handling
fields.description: Market data arrives in contract-specific, venue-specific pieces. This week covers futures specifications, rolls and continuous contracts, forex conventions, tick and bar construction, and cleaning bad data without introducing bias.

fields.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
fields.description: Before any finance-specific model, you need the core supervised learning toolkit. This week covers the bias-variance trade-off, regularized linear models, tree ensembles, time-safe feature engineering, and honest evaluation.

fields.name: Deep Learning and Sequence Models
fields.description: Deep learning helps most with sequences and unstructured data, such as order-book snapshots and text. This week covers network mechanics, PyTorch training, recurrent models, attention, and the techniques that keep training stable.

fields.name: Machine Learning for Finance
fields.description: Finance changes the rules for machine learning. Labels overlap, data is scarce, and backtests overfit easily. This week covers labeling events, purged validation, meta-labeling, multiple-testing corrections, and regime models.

fields.name: Performance Engineering and Backtesting
fields.description: A backtest is useful only if it runs fast enough to iterate on and stays honest about costs and timing. This week covers profiling, compiled kernels, data layout, event-driven simulation, and the realism checks that keep backtests from misleading.

fields.name: Capstone, LLMs for Financial Text, and Interview Preparation
fields.description: This week ties the roadmap together. You scope one capstone project that combines connectivity, data and modeling, evaluate a language model on financial text, and practice the problem types that quant interviews use.

Learning objectives

  • Compute conditional probabilities and apply Bayes' rule to a market signal.
  • Calculate expectation and variance for discrete and continuous random variables.
  • State the assumptions behind the binomial, Poisson and normal models.

Subtopics

1. Sample spaces and conditioning

A probability model begins with a sample space and assigns probabilities to events. Conditional probability, P(A given B), equals P(A and B) divided by P(B), and it is defined only when P(B) is positive. In trading, this answers questions such as how likely an uptick is after the spread widens.

2. Bayes' rule

Bayes' rule inverts a conditional probability. It combines a prior belief about a signal with the evidence observed so far. Quant teams use it to shrink noisy hit-rate estimates toward a sensible prior, which is safer than trusting a small sample.

3. Expectation and variance

Expectation is the probability-weighted average outcome. Linearity of expectation holds even when variables are dependent, which makes it useful for expected P&L across correlated positions. Variance does not add for dependent variables, so covariance must be included explicitly.

4. Core distributions

The binomial model counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials. The Poisson model counts rare events per interval, such as order arrivals in a short window. The normal model is the continuous baseline. Each carries assumptions that should be checked against data before use.

Mathematical theory

For events A and B with P(B) greater than zero, P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B). For a random variable X, Var(X) = E[X squared] minus (E[X]) squared. For independent X and Y, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y).

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Bayesian hit-rate estimate

Simulate a signal that is right with an unknown probability. Update a Beta prior after each observation and check that the posterior mean converges to the true rate as the sample grows.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
true_p = 0.55
a, b = 1, 1  # uniform Beta(1, 1) prior
for hit in rng.random(500) < true_p:
    a += int(hit)
    b += 1 - int(hit)
print(round(a / (a + b), 3))

Experiment 2: Binomial versus Poisson

For large n and small p, compare Binomial(n, p) and Poisson(n times p) probabilities across a grid of n values, and report the largest absolute gap.

Book references

  • Blitzstein and Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press). Read the sections on conditional probability and expectation.
  • Wasserman, All of Statistics (Springer). Compare its probability overview with the course text.

Completion criteria

  • The Experiment 1 posterior mean lands within 0.05 of the true rate after 500 observations for three random seeds.
  • You can explain, without notes, why Var(X + Y) differs from Var(X) + Var(Y) when X and Y are correlated.
  • You score at least 16 of 20 on a self-written quiz covering the four distributions.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • The examples assume independent observations. Real order flow is clustered, so the posterior is optimistic.
  • The Beta prior is a modeling choice, and results depend on it when samples are small.

Learning objectives

  • Estimate parameters and attach uncertainty to them with confidence intervals.
  • Run and interpret hypothesis tests without treating a p-value as a probability that a strategy works.
  • Recognize false discoveries that come from testing many strategies.

Subtopics

1. Estimators and their properties

An estimator is a rule that maps data to a parameter value. The sample mean is unbiased for the expected return, and its error shrinks with the square root of the sample size. Bias, variance and consistency are the properties to check before trusting any estimate.

2. Confidence intervals

A confidence interval is built by a procedure that covers the true parameter in a stated fraction of repeated samples. Bootstrap intervals resample observed returns and recompute the statistic, which avoids some normality assumptions but still assumes independence.

3. Hypothesis tests and p-values

A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true. Research that tests many variants without correction will produce small p-values by chance.

4. Power and sample size

Power is the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size. Small edges need long samples. A strategy with a true annual Sharpe ratio near one often needs several years of daily data before a backtest can separate it from zero with confidence.

Mathematical theory

The standard error of the sample mean is s divided by the square root of n. A one-sample t statistic is (sample mean minus mu0) divided by that standard error.

t = (xbar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n))

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Bootstrap interval for mean daily return

Simulate three years of daily returns, resample them 2000 times, and compare the percentile interval with the analytic interval from the standard error.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
returns = rng.normal(0.0004, 0.01, 750)
boot = [rng.choice(returns, size=returns.size, replace=True).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
print(np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]))

Experiment 2: False-positive rate under the null

Generate 1000 zero-mean strategies, apply a 5 percent t-test to each, and confirm the rejection rate is near 5 percent. Then repeat across 50 strategies with a Bonferroni correction and compare the family-wise error rate.

Book references

  • Wasserman, All of Statistics (Springer). Read the sections on estimation and hypothesis testing.
  • Lo, "The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios" (Financial Analysts Journal, 2002). Read for the standard error of Sharpe estimates.

Completion criteria

  • The bootstrap interval for the mean covers the true value in at least 92 percent of 500 repeated simulations.
  • The Experiment 2 rejection rate lands between 4 and 6 percent, and the corrected family-wise rate is reported.
  • You explain a p-value in one correct sentence without consulting notes.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Daily returns are not independent, so the plain bootstrap understates uncertainty. A block bootstrap is needed for real data.
  • Simulated examples assume a known true mean, which real markets never provide.

fields.topic_name: Law of large numbers and the central limit theorem
fields.description:
Learning objectives

  • State the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem with their conditions.
  • Identify when the normal approximation fails, especially for heavy-tailed data.
  • Build confidence intervals for a sample mean using the central limit theorem.

Subtopics

1. The law of large numbers

The law of large numbers says that a sample average converges to the expected value as the sample grows. It guarantees that a long backtest eventually reflects the true average return, but it says nothing about how fast that happens, and that speed is what matters in practice.

2. The central limit theorem

For independent observations with finite variance, the standardized sample mean approaches a standard normal distribution. This justifies normal-based intervals for averages, which is why it is used so widely in finance, even when the underlying data is not normal.

3. Heavy tails and infinite variance

If the variance is infinite, the central limit theorem does not apply in its standard form. Student-t distributions with few degrees of freedom and Pareto tails are common in financial losses. Sample means then converge slowly, and normal intervals undercover.

4. Dependence and effective sample size

Positive autocorrelation makes averages less precise than the raw sample size suggests. The effective sample size is smaller, so intervals built as if observations were independent are too narrow.

Mathematical theory

If X1 through Xn are independent with mean mu and variance sigma squared, then the quantity sqrt(n) times (xbar minus mu) divided by sigma converges in distribution to a standard normal. For an AR(1) process with coefficient phi, the variance of the sample mean is inflated by the factor (1 + phi) divided by (1 minus phi), relative to independent data.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Coverage of normal intervals for heavy tails

Draw samples of size 30 from a Student-t distribution with 3 degrees of freedom. Build a 95 percent normal interval for the mean in each sample and measure how often it covers the true mean.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
covered = 0
for _ in range(5000):
    x = stats.t.rvs(df=3, size=30, random_state=rng)
    half = 1.96 * x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(30)
    covered += abs(x.mean()) <= half
print(covered / 5000)

Experiment 2: Variance inflation under autocorrelation

Simulate an AR(1) series with phi equal to 0.5, compare the empirical variance of the sample mean with the theoretical inflation factor, and repeat for phi values from 0 to 0.8.

Book references

  • Blitzstein and Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press). Look for the sections on the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.
  • Taleb, The Black Swan (Random House). A non-technical discussion of why fat tails break averages.

Completion criteria

  • Report the empirical coverage from Experiment 1 and state whether it falls below the nominal 95 percent.
  • The empirical variance inflation in Experiment 2 matches the formula within 10 percent for phi equal to 0.5.
  • Write a paragraph stating the two conditions the central limit theorem requires.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Asymptotic results may take many observations to become accurate, and 30 observations is a small sample.
  • The examples use simulated data, so they show mechanisms rather than real market behavior.

Learning objectives

  • Compute log returns and explain why they add over time.
  • Measure skewness and excess kurtosis and compare them with normal values.
  • Fit a Student-t distribution by maximum likelihood and compare tail behavior.

Subtopics

1. Simple versus log returns

Simple returns compound multiplicatively across periods, while log returns add across periods. Log returns are therefore easier to aggregate and model. For small moves the two are nearly equal, which is why the distinction is often ignored in daily work and then matters for long horizons.

2. Stylized facts

Empirical returns show fat tails, volatility clustering, a leverage effect where falling prices raise volatility more than rising prices, and little linear autocorrelation in returns. A model that matches these facts is more useful than one that matches only the mean and variance.

3. Fitting heavy-tailed models

Maximum likelihood fits the degrees of freedom and scale of a Student-t distribution. The fitted degrees of freedom summarize tail weight. Comparing log-likelihoods across the normal and t models shows whether the extra parameter is justified by the data.

4. Tail risk measures

Value at risk at a given confidence level is a quantile of the loss distribution. Comparing the empirical quantile with the normal quantile reveals how much the normal model understates tail losses.

Mathematical theory

The log return is r_t equal to ln(P_t) minus ln(P_t minus 1). The fourth standardized moment is E[(X minus mu) to the fourth] divided by sigma to the fourth. A normal variable has kurtosis 3, so excess kurtosis is zero. A Student-t variable with nu greater than 4 degrees of freedom has excess kurtosis 6 divided by (nu minus 4).

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Excess kurtosis of normal and Student-t returns

Simulate 10000 normal daily returns and 10000 Student-t returns with 4 degrees of freedom, scaled to the same standard deviation. Compare their sample excess kurtosis with the theoretical values of 0 and 6.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
normal_r = rng.normal(0, 0.01, 10_000)
t_r = stats.t.rvs(df=4, scale=0.01 / np.sqrt(2), size=10_000, random_state=1)
print(round(stats.kurtosis(normal_r), 2), round(stats.kurtosis(t_r), 2))

Experiment 2: Maximum likelihood fit

Fit a Student-t distribution to the simulated t sample with scipy.stats.t.fit, recover the degrees of freedom, and compare the log-likelihood with a fitted normal.

Book references

  • Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series (Wiley). Look for the discussion of stylized facts of asset returns.
  • Cont, "Empirical Properties of Asset Returns: Stylized Facts and Statistical Issues" (Quantitative Finance, 2001).

Completion criteria

  • The excess kurtosis of the t(4) sample is within 1.5 of the theoretical value of 6.
  • The fitted degrees of freedom recover a value between 3 and 5 for the simulated sample.
  • You explain in writing why log returns can be summed across days.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Daily return samples are noisy, and kurtosis estimates are unstable without many observations.
  • Student-t fits assume independent observations, which volatility clustering violates.

Learning objectives

  • Estimate expectations by simulation and report the standard error with each estimate.
  • Apply antithetic variates to reduce the variance of a Monte Carlo estimate.
  • Check a simulation against a closed-form price.

Subtopics

1. Simulation as estimation

A Monte Carlo estimate averages a function of simulated random draws. By the law of large numbers, the average converges to the expected value. The standard error falls with the square root of the number of paths, which is slow, so efficiency techniques matter.

2. Random number generation and seeding

Pseudorandom generators are deterministic given a seed. Fixing the seed makes results reproducible. Use one generator object per experiment and pass it explicitly, rather than relying on global state, so that independent runs do not share streams.

3. Variance reduction

Antithetic variates pair each draw with its negative, which induces negative correlation between paired outcomes. Control variates subtract a term with a known expectation that is correlated with the target. Both reduce error without more paths.

4. Pricing by simulation

Under the risk-neutral measure, a derivative price is the discounted expected payoff. Simulating the underlying under that measure and averaging the discounted payoffs gives an estimate that should match the Black-Scholes formula for a European call.

Mathematical theory

Estimate the expectation of f(X) with the average of f(X_i) over N draws. The standard error is the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of N. Under geometric Brownian motion, the terminal price is S_T equal to S_0 times exp of ((r minus sigma squared over 2) T plus sigma times the square root of T times Z), where Z is standard normal.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: European call by simulation

Estimate the price of an at-the-money call, report the standard error, and compare it with the closed-form Black-Scholes value.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
S0, K, r, sigma, T, N = 100.0, 100.0, 0.02, 0.2, 1.0, 100_000
z = rng.standard_normal(N)
ST = S0 * np.exp((r - 0.5 * sigma**2) * T + sigma * np.sqrt(T) * z)
payoff = np.exp(-r * T) * np.maximum(ST - K, 0.0)
print(payoff.mean(), payoff.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N))

Experiment 2: Antithetic variates

Rerun Experiment 1 using the draws z and negative z together, and compare the standard error with the plain estimate at the same number of total evaluations.

Book references

  • Glasserman, Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering (Springer). Read the chapters on variance reduction and path generation.
  • Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Pearson). Use the Black-Scholes formula as the reference value.

Completion criteria

  • The Monte Carlo price lies within three standard errors of the Black-Scholes price.
  • You report standard errors with and without antithetic variates and state the reduction factor.
  • Your notebook reproduces the same numbers when run twice with the same seed.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Constant volatility and the geometric Brownian motion model are assumptions. Real option prices show a volatility smile.
  • Estimates of tail probabilities need far more paths than estimates of means.

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish stationary from non-stationary series using summary statistics and unit-root tests.
  • Read autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots to choose candidate models.
  • Explain why prices are usually non-stationary while returns are close to stationary.

Subtopics

1. Weak stationarity

A weakly stationary series has a constant mean, a constant variance, and an autocovariance that depends only on the lag. Most econometric methods assume this property. A price series that trends or wanders does not satisfy it, so models built on raw prices give misleading results.

2. Unit roots and the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test

A unit root means shocks persist forever, as in a random walk. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test regresses the first difference of a series on its lagged level and tests whether the coefficient is zero. Rejecting the null suggests stationarity, but the test has low power when the process is close to a unit root.

3. Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation

The autocorrelation function measures the correlation between a series and its lagged values. The partial autocorrelation removes the effect of intermediate lags. Their patterns guide the choice of autoregressive and moving-average orders in later models.

4. Returns versus prices

Differencing a price series produces returns, which are much closer to stationary. Working with returns is standard, but it discards information about levels, which matters for mean reversion and cointegration in later topics.

Mathematical theory

The lag-k autocorrelation is rho_k equal to Cov(X_t, X_(t minus k)) divided by Var(X_t). The Augmented Dickey-Fuller regression is the first difference of y_t equal to a constant plus gamma times y_(t minus 1) plus an error term, and the null hypothesis is that gamma equals zero.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Unit-root test on a random walk and its returns

Simulate a random-walk price path and compare the Augmented Dickey-Fuller p-values for the levels and the first differences across several seeds.

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
prices = 100 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, 1000))
returns = np.diff(prices)
print("levels p-value:", round(adfuller(prices)[1], 3))
print("returns p-value:", round(adfuller(returns)[1], 3))

Experiment 2: Autocorrelation of returns and squared returns

Compute the autocorrelation of returns and of squared returns for a real or sample index. Returns should show little autocorrelation, while squared returns often show persistent autocorrelation, which is the signature of volatility clustering.

Book references

  • Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (OTexts). Read the section on stationarity and differencing.
  • Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series (Wiley). Read the early chapters on stationarity and linear time series.

Completion criteria

  • The Experiment 1 levels p-value is above 0.1 and the returns p-value is below 0.05 for five seeds.
  • You identify the lag at which the partial autocorrelation cuts off for a simulated AR(2) series.
  • You write two sentences explaining why returns are preferred to prices for modeling.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test has low power near a unit root and can miss slow mean reversion.
  • Structural breaks, such as a change in market regime, can make a stationary series look non-stationary.

Learning objectives

  • Specify autoregressive, moving-average and integrated components in an ARIMA model.
  • Select model orders with information criteria and residual diagnostics.
  • Evaluate forecasts with rolling out-of-sample windows against a naive benchmark.

Subtopics

1. Autoregressive and moving-average terms

An autoregressive term expresses today's value as a weighted sum of past values plus noise. A moving-average term expresses it as a weighted sum of past shocks. Combining both in an ARMA model captures a wide range of linear dynamics in stationary data.

2. Differencing and the integrated component

Differencing a series d times removes a unit root, which is what the integrated part of ARIMA does. Over-differencing introduces artificial negative autocorrelation, so the order d should be justified by a unit-root test rather than chosen by habit.

3. Order selection and diagnostics

Akaike and Bayesian information criteria balance fit against complexity. After fitting, residuals should look like white noise. The Ljung-Box test checks for remaining autocorrelation, and a small p-value signals a misspecified model.

4. Rolling forecast evaluation

Refit the model on a rolling window, forecast one step ahead, and record the error. Compare the root mean squared error with a naive forecast that predicts zero change. For financial returns, the naive benchmark is hard to beat.

Mathematical theory

An AR(1) process is x_t equal to phi times x_(t minus 1) plus e_t, which is stationary when the absolute value of phi is less than one. The ARIMA(p, d, q) model applies the differencing operator d times, then fits an ARMA(p, q) model to the result.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Recover an AR(1) coefficient

Simulate an AR(1) series with phi equal to 0.6, fit an ARIMA(1, 0, 0) model, and check that the estimate is close to the true value.

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
e = rng.normal(size=600)
x = np.zeros(600)
for t in range(1, 600):
    x[t] = 0.6 * x[t - 1] + e[t]
fit = ARIMA(x, order=(1, 0, 0)).fit()
print(round(fit.params[1], 3))

Experiment 2: Rolling forecast against a naive benchmark

Using a 250-observation window, forecast each next value with ARIMA and with a zero-change rule, and compare root mean squared errors. Report both numbers and the difference.

Book references

  • Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (OTexts). Read the chapter on ARIMA models.
  • Box, Jenkins, Reinsel and Ljung, Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control (Wiley). The original reference for the methodology.

Completion criteria

  • The recovered AR coefficient is within 0.05 of the true value of 0.6.
  • The Ljung-Box p-value on the residuals is above 0.05 for the fitted model.
  • The rolling evaluation reports both RMSE values, and you state which forecast wins.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • ARIMA is linear and assumes a stable structure. Financial regimes change, and rolling windows only partly adapt.
  • Forecasting returns with ARIMA usually produces a forecast close to the mean, which is an honest result and not a failure.

Learning objectives

  • Describe volatility clustering and why constant-variance models fail for daily returns.
  • Write the GARCH(1,1) recursion and interpret its parameters.
  • Forecast volatility and use the forecasts for a value-at-risk estimate.

Subtopics

1. Volatility clustering

Large moves tend to follow large moves, and calm periods tend to persist. This pattern appears in squared and absolute returns even when the returns themselves are uncorrelated. A model of time-varying variance captures it.

2. The GARCH(1,1) recursion

Today's variance depends on a constant, yesterday's squared shock, and yesterday's variance. The alpha parameter measures how strongly new shocks feed into variance, and beta measures how long shocks persist. Their sum, the persistence, controls how quickly volatility returns to its long-run level.

3. Variants for asymmetry

Leverage effects mean that negative shocks raise volatility more than positive shocks. GJR-GARCH and exponential GARCH add terms that allow asymmetric responses. Comparing them with plain GARCH shows whether asymmetry matters for the index studied.

4. Forecasting and risk

A fitted GARCH model produces multi-step variance forecasts that converge to the long-run variance. Combining the one-day forecast with a distributional assumption gives a value-at-risk estimate, which can be checked against realized exceedances.

Mathematical theory

The variance recursion is sigma_t squared equal to omega plus alpha times the squared shock at t minus 1, plus beta times sigma squared at t minus 1. When alpha plus beta is below one, the unconditional variance is omega divided by (1 minus alpha minus beta).

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Simulate and recover a GARCH(1,1) process

Simulate 2000 observations with known parameters, then fit a GARCH(1,1) model and check that the estimated persistence is close to the true value.

import numpy as np
from arch import arch_model
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, omega, alpha, beta = 2000, 0.05, 0.08, 0.90
sig2 = np.empty(n)
eps = np.empty(n)
sig2[0] = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
eps[0] = rng.normal() * np.sqrt(sig2[0])
for t in range(1, n):
    sig2[t] = omega + alpha * eps[t - 1] ** 2 + beta * sig2[t - 1]
    eps[t] = rng.normal() * np.sqrt(sig2[t])
res = arch_model(eps, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1).fit(disp="off")
print(res.params.round(3))

Experiment 2: Value-at-risk backtest

Use a rolling window to forecast one-day 99 percent value at risk from a GARCH model, count the days when losses exceed the forecast, and compare the exceedance rate with the nominal 1 percent.

Book references

  • Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series (Wiley). Read the chapter on conditional heteroscedastic models.
  • Bollerslev, "Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity" (Journal of Econometrics, 1986). The original GARCH paper.

Completion criteria

  • The estimated alpha plus beta is within 0.03 of the true value of 0.98.
  • The Experiment 2 exceedance rate is within one percentage point of the nominal 1 percent.
  • You explain persistence in one paragraph without referring to notes.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Normal innovations understate tail risk. A Student-t distribution is usually a better choice for daily data.
  • Parameters drift over time, so a fixed estimate can become stale during stress periods.

Learning objectives

  • Describe a random walk and show how its scaled limit becomes Brownian motion.
  • Write geometric Brownian motion and derive its solution for the price.
  • Estimate drift and volatility from simulated price paths and assess the estimation error.

Subtopics

1. The symmetric random walk

A random walk adds independent steps to a starting value. Its variance grows linearly with the number of steps, so the typical distance from the start grows with the square root of time. This is the discrete model that underlies most continuous-time price models.

2. Brownian motion as a limit

Rescaling a random walk in time and space gives Brownian motion, a process with independent normal increments and continuous paths. Its variance at time t equals t, and this scaling property is used throughout stochastic calculus.

3. Geometric Brownian motion

Geometric Brownian motion models a price whose log return is normal. Its drift controls the average growth, and its volatility controls the spread. The solution is an exponential of a Brownian motion, which keeps prices positive.

4. Estimating drift and volatility

Volatility can be estimated from the standard deviation of log returns, scaled by the square root of the time step. Drift estimates are much noisier, because the sample mean error shrinks slowly. Long histories are needed before the drift estimate is informative.

Mathematical theory

Brownian motion W_t is normal with mean zero and variance t. Geometric Brownian motion satisfies dS equal to mu times S times dt plus sigma times S times dW, with solution S_t equal to S_0 times exp of ((mu minus sigma squared over 2) times t plus sigma times W_t).

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Recover drift and volatility from a simulated path

Simulate ten years of daily log returns from a known geometric Brownian motion, estimate volatility from the standard deviation, and estimate drift from the mean.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
mu, sigma, dt, n = 0.08, 0.2, 1 / 252, 252 * 10
r = (mu - 0.5 * sigma**2) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal(n)
sigma_hat = r.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(dt)
mu_hat = r.mean() / dt + 0.5 * sigma_hat**2
print(round(sigma_hat, 3), round(mu_hat, 3))

Experiment 2: Brownian scaling

Simulate 1000 random walks of 500 steps and check that the cross-sectional variance at step t grows linearly with t.

Book references

  • Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II: Continuous-Time Models (Springer). Read the early chapters on Brownian motion.
  • Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (Pearson). Read the discussion of stock price models.

Completion criteria

  • The volatility estimate from Experiment 1 is within 0.01 of the true value of 0.2.
  • The variance check in Experiment 2 is within 5 percent of linear growth.
  • You explain in one paragraph why the drift estimate has a large error over ten years.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Constant drift and volatility are assumptions. Real prices show jumps and changing volatility.
  • Discretization introduces error at coarse time steps, and daily data hides intraday behavior.

Learning objectives

  • Explain why regressing one trending series on another can produce spurious results.
  • Test a pair of series for cointegration using the Engle-Granger procedure.

Subtopics

1. Spurious regression

Two independent random walks often produce a high R-squared and significant coefficients when regressed on each other. The results look meaningful but are artifacts of shared trends. Recognizing this pattern is the first step toward valid pairs analysis.

2. Cointegration

Two series are cointegrated when a linear combination of them is stationary. The combination is the spread, and its stationarity means the two series share a long-run equilibrium, even though each one wanders.

3. The Engle-Granger procedure

First regress one series on the other to estimate the hedge ratio. Then test the residual spread for a unit root with an adjusted critical value. The adjustment is needed because the residuals come from an estimated regression.

4. Half-life of mean reversion

Modeling the spread as an autoregressive process gives a half-life, the expected time for a deviation to shrink by half. Half-life guides holding periods and helps judge whether a pair is tradable within a reasonable time.

Mathematical theory

The spread is s_t equal to y_t minus beta times x_t. An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process for the spread has mean reversion speed theta, and its half-life is ln(2) divided by theta. In discrete time, if the spread follows an AR(1) with coefficient phi, the half-life is minus ln(2) divided by ln(phi).

Subtopics

1. Vectors, inner products and matrix products

An inner product multiplies and sums matching entries of two vectors. A matrix product stacks inner products of rows and columns. Portfolio returns, regression predictions and factor exposures are all written this way, so fluency in shapes is essential.

2. Solving linear systems

Solving a system is almost always faster and more accurate with a dedicated solver than with an explicit inverse. The normal equations for regression are a standard example, and the solver form avoids squaring the condition number.

3. Rank and conditioning

A matrix has full rank when its columns are linearly independent. Near-collinear columns make the matrix ill-conditioned, so small data errors produce large coefficient changes. The condition number measures this sensitivity.

4. Transposes and symmetric matrices

Covariance matrices and Gram matrices are symmetric, which gives them useful properties such as real eigenvalues. Recognizing symmetry lets you choose faster and more stable algorithms.

Mathematical theory

Ordinary least squares gives beta equal to the inverse of X transpose X, times X transpose y. Numerically this is computed by solving (X transpose X) beta equal to X transpose y. The condition number of a matrix is the ratio of its largest to smallest singular value, and squaring the design matrix squares this ratio.

Subtopics

1. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction that the matrix only stretches, and the eigenvalue is the stretch factor. For a symmetric covariance matrix, eigenvectors are orthogonal and eigenvalues are real and nonnegative, which gives a clean decomposition of risk into independent directions.

2. The singular value decomposition

Any matrix factors as U times Sigma times V transpose, where the singular values in Sigma are the square roots of the eigenvalues of X transpose X. The SVD works for non-square matrices and is numerically more stable than forming covariance matrices.

3. Principal component analysis

Principal components are the right singular vectors of the centered return matrix. The first components capture the directions of largest common variation, often market or sector factors. The explained-variance ratio tells how many components are needed.

4. Truncation and denoising

Keeping only the largest singular values reconstructs a matrix with less noise. This is useful for denoising covariance estimates, but it discards information if the cut is too aggressive.

Mathematical theory

An eigenvector v and eigenvalue lambda satisfy A v equal to lambda v. The SVD of a centered data matrix X is X equal to U Sigma V transpose. The share of variance explained by the first k components is the sum of the first k squared singular values divided by the total sum of squared singular values.

Subtopics

1. The sample covariance matrix

The sample covariance averages outer products of demeaned returns. It is unbiased for the population covariance under standard assumptions, but it has many entries, and each one is estimated from the same limited history.

2. Estimation error and dimension

With N assets and T observations, the sample covariance has N times (N plus 1) divided by 2 unique parameters. When N is close to T, many eigenvalues are biased, and the estimate becomes unstable in optimization.

3. Shrinkage estimators

Shrinkage blends the sample covariance with a structured target, such as a constant-correlation matrix. The blend weight is chosen to minimize expected estimation error. The result is better conditioned and produces more stable portfolios.

4. Use in portfolio construction

Mean-variance optimizers are sensitive to small changes in covariance, so estimation error can dominate the result. Shrinkage is a standard defense, and comparing out-of-sample risk shows whether it helps for a given universe.

Mathematical theory

The sample covariance is S equal to the sum of demeaned outer products divided by T minus 1. A shrunk estimate is delta times a target F plus (1 minus delta) times S, where delta lies between zero and one and is chosen by the estimator.

Subtopics

1. Arrays versus Python lists

A NumPy array stores values of one type in a contiguous block of memory. Operations run in compiled code over the whole block, which avoids the per-element overhead of Python. This is the main reason numerical code should be vectorized.

2. Broadcasting

Broadcasting lets operations combine arrays of different shapes by stretching size-one dimensions. Standardizing each column of a matrix by subtracting a row of means is a standard use. Misunderstood broadcasting is a common source of silent bugs.

3. Universal functions and reductions

Universal functions apply element by element, and reductions such as sum and mean collapse an axis. Choosing the correct axis is essential. Chaining these operations often replaces an entire loop with one expression.

4. Views, copies and memory

Slicing returns a view that shares memory with the original, so modifying the view changes the original. Fancy indexing returns a copy. Knowing which is which prevents both hidden bugs and unnecessary memory use.

Mathematical theory

A rolling mean of width w can be computed from a cumulative sum: the mean at position i equals the difference of cumulative sums at i plus w and at i, divided by w. This reduces the cost from order n times w to order n.

Subtopics

1. DatetimeIndex and time zones

A DatetimeIndex lets pandas align, slice and resample by time. Market data should be stored with a timezone, because exchange hours differ across venues. Mixing naive and aware timestamps is a frequent source of silent misalignment.

2. Resampling

Resampling aggregates observations into regular bars. The aggregation rule matters: the last price is the usual close, while volume should be summed. Labels and closed intervals should be checked so that each bar uses only data available at its close.

3. Missing values

Forward filling carries the last known value forward and is safe for prices because it uses only past data. Dropping rows changes the sample, and interpolation can use future values. Each choice should be documented and tested.

4. Alignment without look-ahead

Joining a slow series, such as quotes, onto a faster series, such as trades, should use the most recent quote at or before each trade. The merge-asof operation does exactly this and prevents accidental use of future information.

Mathematical theory

For a resampled bar with closing price at time T, the bar's close is the last trade at or before T. An as-of join selects, for each trade time t, the quote with the largest timestamp less than or equal to t. This is a form of conditioning on the information set available at time t.

Subtopics

1. Tag=value encoding

A FIX message is a sequence of tag=value pairs separated by the SOH control character, which has ASCII code 1. Tags are integers defined by the specification, and values are typed. This compact encoding is easy to parse but unforgiving of malformed input.

2. Header, body and trailer

The header carries BeginString (tag 8), BodyLength (tag 9), MsgType (tag 35), MsgSeqNum (tag 34), SenderCompID (tag 49), TargetCompID (tag 56) and SendingTime (tag 52). The body holds message-specific fields, and the trailer holds CheckSum (tag 10).

3. BodyLength and CheckSum

BodyLength counts the bytes from after the BodyLength field up to and including the SOH before the CheckSum field. CheckSum is the sum of all bytes before the tag 10 field, modulo 256, written as three digits. Receivers reject messages whose values do not match.

4. Data types and repeating groups

Fields have types such as integer, price, quantity, timestamp and character. Repeating groups carry lists of entries, such as market data levels, with a count field that tells the parser how many entries follow.

Mathematical theory

If B is the byte string from the first byte after the BodyLength field up to the last SOH before tag 10, then BodyLength equals the length of B. The CheckSum equals the sum of byte values of all bytes before the tag 10 field, modulo 256.

Subtopics

1. Logon and heartbeats

A session begins with a Logon message that sets the heartbeat interval. Each side sends a Heartbeat after silence for that interval. Missing heartbeats trigger a TestRequest, and no reply means the connection should be treated as broken.

2. Sequence numbers

Each message carries MsgSeqNum (tag 34), and each side expects the next number in order. A higher number than expected reveals a gap. A lower number that was already processed signals a duplicate, which must be discarded rather than applied twice.

3. Resend requests and gap fill

A ResendRequest asks the counterparty to replay a range of messages. Administrative messages can be replaced by a SequenceReset in gap-fill mode, which advances the counter without replaying them. Application messages such as orders must be replayed in full.

4. Logout and session reset

A Logout ends the session cleanly. Resetting sequence numbers to one discards the recovery mechanism, so it should happen only under an agreed procedure and with a record of the open orders at that time.

Mathematical theory

Let the expected sequence number be E and the received number be S. If S equals E, the message is processed and E advances by one. If S is greater than E, the messages from E through S minus 1 are missing. If S is less than E, the message is a duplicate or a protocol error.

Subtopics

1. New orders

A NewOrderSingle (MsgType D) carries a ClOrdID (tag 11) chosen by the client, the side (tag 54), the quantity (tag 38), the order type (tag 40) and, for limit orders, the price (tag 44). The ClOrdID must be unique within the session, because it links every later message to the order.

2. Cancels and replaces

An OrderCancelRequest (MsgType F) asks to cancel an open order. An OrderCancelReplaceRequest (MsgType G) changes quantity or price. Each request uses a new ClOrdID and references the original through OrigClOrdID, which lets the venue match them.

3. Execution reports

An ExecutionReport (MsgType 8) is the venue's update on an order. ExecType (tag 150) says what happened, such as a new acknowledgment, a fill or a cancel. OrdStatus (tag 39) gives the order's resulting state. ExecID (tag 17) identifies the report itself.

4. Order states and transitions

An order moves from new to partially filled to filled, or to canceled or rejected. Some transitions are illegal, such as a fill after a final cancel. A correct client rejects illegal transitions and flags them for review.

Mathematical theory

The open quantity after each fill equals the order quantity minus the cumulative filled quantity. An order is final when the open quantity is zero or when it is canceled or rejected. Reports for final orders should not change the state.

Subtopics

1. Golden-file replay

A golden file stores the expected output for a captured input. Replaying the input and comparing hashes detects any change in behavior after a code update. This is a simple and strong regression test for protocol code.

2. Simulated disconnects

A disconnect injected at a chosen sequence number tests whether the session recovers. The test should confirm that the resend fills the gap and that no order is sent twice after reconnecting.

3. Idempotent order handling

Retried orders must carry the same ClOrdID, and the system must recognize a retry as the same order. Without this, a timeout can cause a double position. Idempotency is the core safety property of reconnect logic.

4. Certification with the venue

Venues run user-acceptance environments where a firm proves its messages, sequences and recovery behave correctly. Passing those tests is a prerequisite for production access, and simulator success alone does not satisfy it.

Mathematical theory

A replay test is deterministic when the system has no hidden state. A hash comparison of the output sequence is equal across runs if and only if the output sequences are identical, up to the collision resistance of the hash.

Subtopics

1. Bid and ask sides

A limit order book holds resting buy orders on the bid side and resting sell orders on the ask side, each organized by price level. Incoming orders match against the opposite side. The book is the full state of the market at any moment, and everything else is derived from it.

2. Price-time priority

At a given price, earlier orders are filled before later ones. This rule rewards early placement and makes queue position valuable. Strategies that post passive orders must consider where they sit in the queue.

3. Spread and depth

The spread is the gap between the best ask and the best bid, and it measures the cost of immediate execution. Depth is the quantity available near the top of the book. Together they describe liquidity, which changes quickly around news and at the open and close.

4. Mid price and microprice

The mid price is the average of the best bid and ask. The microprice weights each side by the opposite size, which often moves toward the side where more pressure exists. The gap between microprice and mid carries short-term information about direction.

Mathematical theory

The spread equals the best ask minus the best bid. The mid price equals the sum of the best bid and best ask divided by two. A simple microprice is the best ask times the bid size, plus the best bid times the ask size, all divided by the sum of the two sizes.

Subtopics

1. Market and limit orders

A market order executes immediately at the best available prices and accepts the cost of crossing the spread. A limit order sets a maximum buy or minimum sell price, and it may wait in the book. The choice is a trade-off between certainty of fill and price.

2. Time-in-force instructions

Immediate-or-cancel orders fill what they can and cancel the rest. Fill-or-kill orders execute entirely or not at all. Good-till-canceled orders rest until filled or canceled. These instructions shape how an order interacts with the book.

3. Stop orders

A stop order becomes a market or limit order once the price reaches a trigger. Stops can accelerate moves because triggered orders add to the same direction of pressure. Stop-limit orders avoid bad fills but may never execute.

4. Queue position and fill probability

A passive order fills only after the orders ahead of it at the same price are filled or canceled. Fill probability therefore depends on the queue length and the rate at which orders ahead are consumed. Estimating this helps decide between waiting and crossing the spread.

Mathematical theory

If a passive order has Q orders ahead and the queue ahead is consumed at a rate of lambda per unit time, the expected waiting time before the order reaches the front is roughly Q divided by lambda. Real queues have arrivals and cancellations, so this is a rough guide and not a precise result.

Subtopics

1. Temporary and permanent impact

Temporary impact is the price concession paid while an order executes and that reverts afterward. Permanent impact is the part that persists because the trade revealed information or changed inventory. Execution models treat the two differently.

2. Implementation shortfall

Implementation shortfall measures the gap between the decision price and the final average execution price. It splits into delay cost from the time before trading, trading cost from market impact during execution, and opportunity cost from unfilled quantity.

3. The square-root law

Empirical studies find that impact grows roughly with the square root of the order size relative to daily volume, scaled by volatility. The law is a heuristic that works across many markets, but its constant must be estimated for each market and period.

4. Optimal execution trade-offs

Trading fast reduces price risk but increases impact. Trading slowly does the reverse. Optimal execution models choose a schedule that balances these two costs, given a risk-aversion parameter.

Mathematical theory

A common square-root approximation is impact equal to a constant k times volatility times the square root of order size divided by daily volume. Taking logarithms gives a linear relation, so the exponent can be estimated by ordinary regression. An exponent near one half is consistent with the square-root law.

Subtopics

1. Size and notional limits

Quantity and notional limits stop an order that is too large in shares or in value. They catch input errors such as a misplaced decimal. Limits should be set per account and per instrument, based on expected activity.

2. Price-band checks

A price-band check rejects orders priced too far from a reference price, such as the last trade or a prior close. This is the usual defense against fat-finger errors. The band width should reflect normal volatility in the instrument.

3. Position and credit limits

Position limits cap the net exposure in an instrument, and credit limits cap the exposure to a counterparty or account. Checks must include working orders, not only filled positions, because open orders can add exposure if they fill.

4. Kill switches and idempotency

A kill switch halts all new order submission and can cancel working orders. Idempotent submission means a retried order carries the same client identifier, so the venue or the gateway recognizes it as a duplicate. The rule protects against double exposure after a timeout.

Mathematical theory

A price-band check accepts an order when the absolute difference between the order price and the reference price, divided by the reference price, is no larger than the band fraction. A notional check compares quantity times price with a maximum notional value. Both checks are simple inequalities, so their correctness is tested by boundary cases.

Subtopics

1. Present value of cash flows

A bond is a set of future coupons and a principal repayment. Its price is the sum of each cash flow discounted at a rate that reflects time and risk. Changing the discount rate changes the price in the opposite direction, which is the basis of all fixed income risk measures.

2. Yield to maturity

Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates the bond's price with the present value of its cash flows. It has no closed form for coupon bonds, so it is found numerically. Yield is a convenient summary, but it assumes that coupons can be reinvested at the same rate.

3. Clean and dirty prices

Quoted prices are usually clean, meaning they exclude interest accrued since the last coupon. The invoice price, called the dirty price, adds accrued interest. Trades settle at the dirty price, so accrued interest must be computed correctly.

4. Day count conventions

Conventions such as actual over 360, actual over actual, and 30 over 360 determine how accrued interest and periods are counted. Using the wrong convention gives small but systematic pricing errors, which matter at scale.

Mathematical theory

With coupon C, face value F, m coupons per year and n years, the price at yield y is the sum over k from 1 to n times m of C divided by (1 plus y over m) to the power k, plus F divided by (1 plus y over m) to the power n times m. The dirty price equals the clean price plus accrued interest.

Subtopics

1. Modified duration

Modified duration measures the percentage price sensitivity to a small change in yield. It is the most common risk measure for bonds. A bond with a duration of five loses roughly five percent of its value when yields rise by one percentage point.

2. DV01

DV01 is the dollar change in price for a one basis point move in yield. Traders use it because it is additive across positions and easy to aggregate. It is the natural unit for hedging and limit setting.

3. Convexity

Convexity captures the curvature of the price-yield relationship. Duration alone understates prices after large yield falls and overstates losses after large rises. Positive convexity is generally valuable to the holder, which is why it carries a cost.

4. Duration hedging

A duration-matched hedge uses an instrument with offsetting sensitivity. Matching DV01 reduces exposure to parallel shifts but not to changes in curve shape. Hedges must be rebalanced as yields and maturities change.

Mathematical theory

Modified duration equals minus one over the price times the derivative of price with respect to yield. A second-order approximation of the percentage price change is minus modified duration times the yield change, plus one half times convexity times the squared yield change. DV01 equals modified duration times price times 0.0001.

Subtopics

1. Zero rates and discount factors

A zero rate is the yield on a single cash flow at a given maturity. Its discount factor is the present value of one unit paid at that maturity. The curve is the set of discount factors or zero rates across maturities, and it is the foundation of all pricing.

2. Bootstrapping from par instruments

A par swap rate has a value of zero, so its annual payments can be used to solve for each discount factor in turn. Each new maturity adds one unknown, which makes the procedure sequential. Errors in early points propagate to later ones.

3. Interpolation

Points between pillars need an interpolation rule. Linear interpolation of zero rates is simple but can create unstable forwards. Log-linear interpolation of discount factors gives piecewise-constant forward rates, which are more stable.

4. Forward rates

A forward rate is the rate implied for a future period by today's curve. It is the quantity that determines the pricing of forward and futures contracts. Negative or spiky forwards often reveal an interpolation problem rather than a market fact.

Mathematical theory

A discount factor and zero rate for maturity T satisfy DF(T) equal to one over (one plus z(T)) to the power T. For an annual par swap with rate s and maturity n, the discount factors satisfy one minus DF(n) equal to s times the sum of DF(k) for k from one to n.

Subtopics

1. Swap structure

In a plain interest rate swap, one party pays a fixed rate and receives a floating rate on the same notional. Only the net payment is exchanged on each date. The contract starts with zero value when its fixed rate equals the par swap rate.

2. Valuing the legs

The floating leg of a single-curve swap is worth the notional times one minus the final discount factor. The fixed leg is worth the fixed rate times the sum of accrual fractions times discount factors, times notional. The swap value is the difference between the two.

3. Rate futures and convexity

Futures are settled daily, while forwards settle once. When rates are correlated with the discount factors used for settlement, the futures rate differs from the forward rate. The gap is the convexity adjustment, which grows with maturity and rate volatility.

4. Using swaps in risk management

Firms use swaps to convert floating-rate exposure into fixed-rate exposure, or the reverse. The hedge ratio depends on the swap's DV01 relative to the exposure, and it must be monitored as the curve moves.

Mathematical theory

For a receiver swap with notional N, fixed rate K and accrual fractions tau, the value is N times one minus DF(n) minus N times K times the sum of tau times DF(k), for k from one to n. A par swap has K equal to the par rate, which makes the value zero.

Subtopics

1. Black-Scholes assumptions

The Black-Scholes model assumes a lognormal price process with constant volatility, continuous trading, no transaction costs and a constant risk-free rate. These assumptions are simplifications, and each one is violated in practice in identifiable ways.

2. Binomial trees

A binomial tree models the price as moving up or down by fixed factors each step. Risk-neutral probabilities make the discounted price a martingale, and backward induction gives the option value. As the number of steps grows, the tree converges to the Black-Scholes price.

3. Implied volatility

Implied volatility is the volatility that makes the Black-Scholes price match the market price. Because the price is monotonic in volatility, a bracketing root finder solves for it reliably. Implied volatilities across strikes form the volatility smile.

4. The Greeks

Delta, gamma, vega, theta and rho measure sensitivities of the option price to the underlying, its curvature, volatility, time and rates. They can be computed analytically under Black-Scholes or by finite differences for any model.

Mathematical theory

The Black-Scholes call price is S times N(d1) minus K times exp(minus r T) times N(d2), where d1 equals (ln(S over K) plus (r plus sigma squared over 2) T) divided by (sigma times the square root of T), and d2 equals d1 minus sigma times the square root of T. N is the standard normal distribution function.

    d2 = d1 - sigma * np.sqrt(T)
    return S * norm.cdf(d1) - K * np.exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)

Subtopics

1. Front month and roll dates

A continuous series follows the front contract until a roll date, then switches to the next contract. Roll dates can be set by calendar, by volume or by open interest. Volume-based rolls follow liquidity, which is usually where trading actually occurs.

2. Additive back-adjustment

Additive adjustment shifts the older prices by the gap between the two contracts at the roll. The result keeps price differences intact and keeps returns close to the raw returns. The disadvantage is that very old prices can become negative for long histories.

3. Ratio back-adjustment

Ratio adjustment multiplies older prices by the ratio of the two contracts at the roll. It preserves percentage returns but changes the price levels in a way that may confuse indicators based on price distance.

4. Effects on backtests

An unadjusted roll creates a false jump in the series, which a strategy can trade on. Each adjustment method changes the historical signal in a different way, so the method must be stated with every backtest result.

Mathematical theory

At a roll, let the old contract's final price be P_old and the new contract's first price be P_new. Additive adjustment adds P_new minus P_old to all earlier prices. Ratio adjustment multiplies all earlier prices by P_new divided by P_old. Either method removes the discontinuity at the roll date.

Subtopics

1. Symbol mapping

Vendors reuse symbols, change them after corporate actions, and retire them without notice. A point-in-time mapping table records which identifier applied on each date. Without it, a history can silently join unrelated instruments.

2. Corporate actions and rolls

Equity splits and dividends change historical prices and must be adjusted to keep returns correct. Futures rolls are a separate adjustment. Each adjustment should be documented and tested against known values.

A dataset that contains only companies still listed today excludes failures and delistings. Strategies tested on it look better than they would have in real time. Point-in-time universes are required for honest research.

4. Detecting bad ticks

Bad ticks are isolated values far from their neighbors. A rolling median provides a robust local level, and the median absolute deviation scales the residuals. Points with large robust z-scores are flagged for review rather than deleted automatically.

For a rolling median m_t and a rolling median absolute deviation D_t of the residuals, the robust z-score is (x_t minus m_t) divided by (1.4826 times D_t). The constant 1.4826 makes the scale consistent with the standard deviation under normality.

Subtopics

1. Regression and classification

Regression predicts a continuous target, such as next-week volatility. Classification predicts a label, such as whether the next day closes up. The loss function should match the goal: squared error for means, log loss for calibrated probabilities.

2. Loss functions

Squared error penalizes large misses heavily, which suits forecasting levels. Log loss penalizes confident wrong probabilities and rewards calibration. Choosing the wrong loss can produce a model that is accurate on average but useless for decisions.

3. Bias and variance

A simple model underfits, which means high bias. A flexible model fits noise, which means high variance. The best model balances the two, and the balance depends on how much data is available.

4. Learning curves and overfitting

A learning curve plots training and validation error against sample size. A large gap that does not close with more data signals overfitting, while two high errors signal underfitting. The curve is the first diagnostic to run.

Mathematical theory

For a squared-error loss, the expected prediction error at a point decomposes into squared bias plus variance plus irreducible noise. Irreducible noise is the part of the target that no function of the inputs can predict.

Subtopics

1. Decision trees

A decision tree splits the data on the feature and threshold that best separate the target. Deep trees fit noise, while shallow trees miss interactions. Trees handle nonlinear relationships and mixed feature types without scaling.

2. Random forests

A random forest averages many trees, each fit on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets. Averaging reduces variance without much added bias, which makes forests a strong default for tabular data.

3. Gradient boosting

Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss, so the ensemble improves step by step. A small learning rate and a moderate number of trees usually generalize better than a large, aggressive model.

4. Feature importance

Impurity importance is biased toward continuous and high-cardinality features. Permutation importance shuffles one feature on held-out data and measures the loss increase. Permutation importance is more reliable, but it can understate correlated features.

Mathematical theory

A boosting model updates its prediction as F_m equal to F_(m minus 1) plus nu times h_m, where h_m is a tree fit to the negative gradient of the loss and nu is the learning rate. The loss for classification is the log loss of the predicted probability.

1. Lagged and rolling features

2. Look-ahead leakage

Leakage happens when a feature uses information from the future relative to the decision. It produces impressive backtests that fail in production. Shifting features by one step before rolling calculations is the simplest guard.

The target should match the holding period and the execution timing. A target built from the same bar used for the feature makes the problem trivially easy. The target should look forward from the decision point, and its horizon should be stated.

Mathematical theory

A feature set is leakage-free if every feature at time t is a function of data observed up to and including time t minus one, when the decision is made at time t. Shifting a series by one step enforces this structure in code.

1. Time-ordered splits

2. Choosing metrics

Log loss measures probability quality, and AUC measures ranking. Precision and recall matter when false signals are costly. A single accuracy number hides the trade-off between these, so report several metrics together.

A calibrated model predicts a probability of 0.6 for events that occur about 60 percent of the time. Calibration curves compare predicted and observed frequencies in bins. Poor calibration can be corrected with isotonic or Platt scaling on validation data.

Log loss for n predictions p_i and outcomes y_i is the negative average of y_i times log p_i plus (1 minus y_i) times log(1 minus p_i). Lower values indicate better probability estimates. Each layer multiplies its input by a weight matrix, adds a bias, and applies a nonlinear activation such as ReLU or a sigmoid. Without the nonlinearity, any stack of layers collapses to a single linear map, so the activation is what gives depth its power.

2. Backpropagation

Backpropagation applies the chain rule backward through the network, reusing intermediate results. It computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight at a cost comparable to a single forward pass, which makes training large models practical.

3. Gradient descent and optimizers

Stochastic gradient descent moves weights against the gradient of a mini-batch loss. Adaptive methods such as Adam scale each parameter's step by running estimates of gradient size. Learning rate and batch size interact strongly, so both must be tuned together.

4. Initialization

Weights that start too large or too small make activations saturate or vanish. Common schemes scale initial weights by the layer's fan-in or fan-out, which keeps signal sizes roughly stable across layers at the start of training.

Mathematical theory

For a single hidden layer, the output is y equal to sigma of W times x plus b, and the chain rule gives the gradient of the loss with respect to W as the outer product of the backpropagated error and the input x. Numerical gradient checks compare this analytic result with central differences.

Subtopics

2. Autograd

Autograd records operations and computes gradients when backward is called. Gradients accumulate across calls, so they must be cleared before each step. Forgetting to clear them is one of the most common training bugs.

3. Modules and data loading

A module packages parameters and the forward computation, and a data loader yields batches. Keeping data preparation separate from the model makes experiments easier to rerun and to test.

Mathematical theory

For a parameter theta and a loss L, autograd computes the vector of partial derivatives of L with respect to theta using the chain rule over the recorded operations. One optimizer step moves theta by the negative learning rate times this gradient, or by an adaptive version of it.

Subtopics

1. Hidden state and sequence modeling

A recurrent network applies the same transformation at every time step and passes a hidden state forward. This lets it model dependence on the past with a fixed number of parameters, regardless of sequence length.

2. Vanishing and exploding gradients

Backpropagation through many steps multiplies many Jacobians together. The product can shrink toward zero or grow without bound. Vanishing gradients stop learning of long-range dependence, and exploding gradients destabilize training.

3. LSTM gates

An LSTM adds a cell state and three gates that control forgetting, writing and output. The cell state carries information with mostly additive updates, which keeps gradients stable over longer spans.

4. Windowed forecasting

A forecasting dataset is built by sliding a window over the series, with each window predicting the next value. Windows must be built only from past values, and the train and test split must respect time order.

Mathematical theory

The forget gate at time t is f_t equal to sigma of W_f times the concatenation of h_(t minus 1) and x_t, plus b_f. The cell update is c_t equal to f_t times c_(t minus 1) plus i_t times g_t, where i_t is the input gate and g_t is a candidate value.

Subtopics

1. Scaled dot-product attention

Each query is compared with every key, the scores are scaled and normalized with a softmax, and the result weights a sum of values. The scaling keeps the scores in a range where the softmax does not saturate.

2. Multi-head attention

Several attention heads run in parallel on different learned projections. Each head can focus on a different kind of relationship, and their outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension.

3. Positional encoding

Attention alone ignores order, so position information is added to the inputs. Sinusoidal and learned encodings are the two common choices. For time series, the time index or a learned embedding plays this role.

4. Cost and scaling

Full attention compares every pair of positions, so its memory and time grow with the square of the sequence length. Parallel computation makes transformers fast on modern hardware, but long sequences need approximations or windowing.

Mathematical theory

Attention of queries Q, keys K and values V equals softmax of Q times K transpose, divided by the square root of the key dimension, times V. Each row of the softmax output sums to one, so each output is a weighted average of the values.

Subtopics

1. Learning rate schedules

A learning rate that is too large makes training diverge, and one that is too small makes it slow. Warmup followed by decay is a common schedule, because the early weights are poorly calibrated and benefit from small steps.

2. Regularization by dropout

Dropout randomly zeroes activations during training, which discourages reliance on any single unit. At test time it is turned off. Its strength is a hyperparameter, and it helps most when data is limited.

3. Normalization layers

Batch normalization and layer normalization rescale activations to stabilize training. Batch normalization depends on batch statistics, which is awkward for small or sequential batches. Layer normalization avoids that dependence.

4. Early stopping and gradient clipping

Early stopping ends training when the validation loss stops improving and keeps the best weights. Gradient clipping limits the norm of the update, which prevents occasional exploding gradients from undoing progress.

Mathematical theory

For the quadratic loss w squared, the gradient is 2w, and one gradient step gives w_new equal to (1 minus 2 times the learning rate) times w. The sequence converges when the absolute value of (1 minus 2 times the learning rate) is below one, which holds for learning rates between zero and one.

Subtopics

1. Fixed-horizon labels and their problems

A label that is the sign of the return over the next N days ignores the path. A trade that rose 10 percent and then fell 12 percent is labeled as a loss even if a stop would have exited earlier. Fixed-horizon labels also ignore volatility, so a quiet day and a volatile day count the same.

2. The triple-barrier method

Each event opens three barriers: an upper profit-taking barrier, a lower stop-loss barrier and a vertical time barrier. The label is the barrier touched first, or zero if the time limit expires. The barriers can scale with recent volatility, so labels adapt to conditions.

3. Overlapping labels and sample weights

When events are sampled frequently, their label windows overlap, and nearby labels share information. Treating them as independent overstates the sample size. Sample weights based on the number of concurrent labels correct for this.

4. Choosing barrier widths

Barrier width determines how often each label occurs and how much noise it carries. Widths tied to volatility keep the balance of labels roughly stable across regimes. The chosen widths must be reported with the results.

Mathematical theory

For an event at time i with entry price p_i, the label is +1 if the first touch of the upper barrier p_i times (1 plus the profit fraction) happens before the lower barrier p_i times (1 minus the stop fraction), and minus one for the reverse. If neither barrier is touched before the time limit, the label is zero.

Subtopics

1. Leakage through overlapping labels

If each label covers the next several days, a training sample just before a test fold can share outcome information with the fold. Ordinary k-fold validation ignores this, so its scores look better than real out-of-sample performance.

2. Purging

Purging removes from the training set any sample whose label window overlaps the test period. The label span must be known for each sample, which is why labeling and validation are designed together.

3. Embargo

Serial dependence in features can leak information across the boundary even after purging. An embargo drops a fixed number of training samples immediately after each test fold, which adds a buffer against that leak.

4. Combinatorial splits

Combinatorial purged cross-validation forms many train and test combinations from the same groups of folds. This produces a distribution of backtest paths rather than a single score, which supports the overfitting checks in a later topic.

Mathematical theory

If a label for sample i spans the interval from time i to time i plus h, then sample i belongs in training only if that interval does not intersect the test interval. The embargo adds a further gap of length e after the test interval before training resumes.

import numpy as np
def purged_splits(n, k, horizon):
    idx = np.arange(n)
    folds = np.array_split(idx, k)
    for test in folds:
        start, end = test[0], test[-1]
        train = idx[(idx < start - horizon) | (idx > end + horizon)]
        yield train, test

Subtopics

1. The primary model

The primary model decides the direction of a trade, for example long or short, and can be simple and interpretable. Its job is to propose candidate trades with a clear rationale.

2. The secondary model

The secondary model learns when the primary model is right. Its target is whether each proposed trade succeeds under the labeling rule. It uses features that describe the state of the market at the moment of the proposal.

3. Precision and recall trade-off

Filtering trades raises precision, which is the share of taken trades that succeed, but lowers recall, which is the share of good opportunities captured. The right balance depends on transaction costs and capital constraints.

4. Bet sizing

The secondary model's probability can scale position size. A fractional Kelly rule is one approach, and it requires the probability to be well calibrated. Oversized bets built on poor probabilities cause large drawdowns.

Mathematical theory

For a binary bet that pays b times the stake when it wins and loses the stake otherwise, the Kelly fraction is p minus (1 minus p) divided by b, where p is the win probability. Fractional Kelly scales this down to limit the risk of estimation error.

Subtopics

1. Multiple testing

If you test many strategies with no real edge, some will look good by chance. The best of them can show a high Sharpe ratio even though every strategy is noise. Reporting only the best result hides how many trials were run.

2. Sharpe ratio uncertainty

The Sharpe ratio is an estimate, and its standard error depends on sample length and on the shape of the return distribution. Short histories give wide intervals, and skewness or kurtosis changes the standard error.

3. The deflated Sharpe ratio

The deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts the observed value for the number of trials, the variance of the trial results and the non-normality of returns. It estimates the probability that the true Sharpe ratio exceeds zero after accounting for selection.

4. Probability of backtest overfitting

This method splits history into subsamples, forms in-sample and out-of-sample combinations, and measures how often the best in-sample strategy ranks poorly out of sample. A high rate signals that the selection process is overfitting.

Mathematical theory

The annualized Sharpe ratio is the mean daily excess return divided by its standard deviation, times the square root of 252. The expected maximum of N independent standard normal draws grows roughly with the square root of twice the logarithm of N, so the best of many noise strategies has a large apparent Sharpe ratio.

Subtopics

1. Regime switching

Markets often switch between calm and stressed periods, and each regime has its own mean and volatility. A single model fit across regimes averages their behavior and can be wrong in both. Regime-aware models describe the switching explicitly.

2. Hidden Markov models

A hidden Markov model assumes an unobserved state follows a Markov chain and that each observation depends on the current state. The observed returns are used to infer which state generated them, and the transition matrix describes how often states change.

3. Estimation with EM

The Baum-Welch algorithm, an instance of expectation-maximization, estimates the transition matrix and the emission parameters together. It can converge to local optima, so several random starts are recommended.

4. Inference and look-ahead

Smoothed state probabilities use the whole sample, including future observations, so they cannot be used for real-time decisions. Filtered probabilities use only past data and are the honest choice for trading. The distinction must be explicit in every backtest.

Mathematical theory

The model has a transition matrix A, where A(i, j) is the probability of moving from state i to state j, and emission distributions that give the density of an observation in each state. The likelihood of the observed sequence is computed with the forward algorithm, and the parameters are updated iteratively.
