Subtopics

1. Measure before optimizing

Intuition about slow code is often wrong. A profile shows the actual distribution of time across functions. Optimizing a function that takes two percent of the runtime cannot improve the total by more than two percent, which is Amdahl's law in practice.

2. Deterministic profiling with cProfile

cProfile records every function call and its duration. It gives exact call counts and cumulative times, but its overhead distorts very short functions. It suits detailed analysis of medium-sized programs.

3. Sampling profilers

py-spy attaches to a running process and samples its call stack at intervals without modifying the code. Its overhead is low, so it suits production-like workloads and long runs, and it can profile processes that are already running.

4. Benchmark hygiene

Benchmarks need warm-up runs, repeated timings, and a record of the machine and Python version. Reporting a single timing from a laptop with other programs running gives numbers that cannot be reproduced.

Mathematical theory

If a fraction f of total runtime is spent in a function and that function is made s times faster, the new total time is (1 minus f) plus f divided by s, relative to the original. Even infinite speedup of a function that takes 10 percent of the time saves at most 10 percent.

slow_sum(2_000_000)
pr.disable()
s = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=s).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(3)
print(s.getvalue()[:300])

Experiment 2: Sampling a running process

Run a long backtest in one terminal and attach py-spy from another terminal, then record which functions appear most often in the samples. Compare the result with the cProfile ranking from Experiment 1.

Book references

  • Gorelick and Ozsvald, High Performance Python (O'Reilly). Read the chapters on profiling.
  • Python documentation for the profile module (docs.python.org). Read the section on the cProfile and pstats modules.

Completion criteria

  • You name the function that dominates the runtime in Experiment 1 and show the profile line that supports it.
  • Experiment 2 produces a sample count per function, and you explain any disagreement with cProfile.
  • Each benchmark you report includes the machine, Python version and number of repeats.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Profiles depend on the workload, so a profile of one input may not represent production traffic.
  • Sampling profilers miss very short functions that run between samples, which makes them less precise for micro-optimizations.

Learning objectives

  • Apply the Numba just-in-time decorator to a numerical loop and verify the output.
  • Separate compilation time from steady-state execution time in a benchmark.
  • Recognize the kinds of Python code that Numba can and cannot compile.

Subtopics

1. Just-in-time compilation

Numba translates a decorated Python function into machine code the first time it is called with a given type signature. Loops over NumPy arrays then run at compiled speed, which often removes the need for a rewrite in another language.

2. Nopython mode and typed code

Nopython mode forbids falling back to Python objects, which guarantees fast code but limits the features allowed. Code that uses simple scalars and arrays compiles best. Dynamic containers and many library calls do not.

3. Warm-up and caching

The first call includes compilation time, which can be seconds. Benchmarks must exclude it. The cache option stores compiled code on disk so that later processes start faster.

4. Limits and alternatives

Numba is not always the fastest option. Vectorized NumPy is often enough, and C extensions or specialized libraries may be better for some kernels. The choice should be guided by profiling results.

Mathematical theory

A moving average of width w can be written as a double loop: for each output position, sum w consecutive values and divide by w. The total work is proportional to n times w, while the cumulative-sum method is proportional to n. Compiled loops reduce the constant factor but not the complexity.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Compiled moving average

Implement a moving average with explicit loops, compile it with Numba, and check that the output matches a NumPy reference to within a small tolerance.

import numpy as np
from numba import njit
@njit(cache=True)
def ma_numba(x, w):
    out = np.empty(x.size - w + 1)
    for i in range(out.size):
        s = 0.0
        for j in range(w):
            s += x[i + j]
        out[i] = s / w
    return out
x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=200_000)
print(ma_numba(x, 20)[:3])

Experiment 2: Warm-up separated from steady state

Time the first call and later calls of the compiled function separately, and report the compilation overhead and the steady-state speedup over pure Python.

Book references

  • Numba documentation (numba.pydata.org). Read the sections on the nopython mode and on performance tips.
  • Gorelick and Ozsvald, High Performance Python (O'Reilly). Read the chapter on compiling with Numba.

Completion criteria

  • The compiled output matches the NumPy reference within 1e-10.
  • Your benchmark reports compile time and steady-state time as separate numbers.
  • You list two Python features that the compiled function avoids and explain why.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Compiled code results can differ slightly from interpreted results because of floating-point ordering, so comparisons use tolerances.
  • Speedups depend on the processor and the array size, and small arrays may not benefit at all.

Learning objectives

  • Explain how row-major and column-major storage affect the speed of array operations.
  • Choose dtypes that balance precision and memory use.
  • Describe the advantages of columnar formats for time series storage.

Subtopics

1. Contiguous memory and strides

NumPy arrays store elements in one block, in row-major or column-major order. Operations that walk along the contiguous direction are fast, because the processor reads neighboring values from cache. Walking across it is slower for large arrays.

2. Choosing dtypes

A float32 array uses half the memory of a float64 array. For many signal computations single precision is adequate, but accumulated sums over long samples may need double precision. The dtype choice should be tested against a reference.

3. Views and copies

Slices and transposes often return views with no copy, while fancy indexing returns a copy. Unnecessary copies double memory use and time. Checking whether an operation returns a view is a simple way to find hidden costs.

4. Columnar storage

Columnar formats such as Parquet and Arrow store each column together, which allows reading only the needed fields and compressing similar values. They suit time series, where queries usually touch a few columns over long ranges.

Mathematical theory

An array of n elements with dtype size b bytes occupies n times b bytes. Converting a float64 array of one billion values to float32 halves the storage from eight gigabytes to four. The memory cost of a copy equals the memory of the array being copied.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Column-major versus row-major summation

Sum the columns of a large matrix stored in two orders and time each case. Report both timings and explain the difference in terms of memory layout.

import numpy as np
import time
A = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(4000, 4000))
Af = np.asfortranarray(A)
def col_sums(M):
    return M.sum(axis=0)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
col_sums(A)
t1 = time.perf_counter()
col_sums(Af)
t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(round(t1 - t0, 4), round(t2 - t1, 4))

Experiment 2: Columnar round trip

Write a one-million-row price table to a columnar file, read back a single column, and compare the file size and read time with a plain CSV of the same data.

Book references

  • Apache Arrow documentation (arrow.apache.org). Read the sections on the columnar format and the Python bindings.
  • Gorelick and Ozsvald, High Performance Python (O'Reilly). Read the chapters on memory and data structures.

Completion criteria

  • Experiment 1 reports both timings on your machine, and you state which layout is faster for column sums.
  • Experiment 2 reports file size and read time for both formats.
  • You compute the memory footprint of your main dataset under float32 and float64.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Timings depend on cache sizes and memory bandwidth, so the exact numbers are specific to the test machine.
  • Lower precision can change results in long accumulations, so any dtype change must be validated.

Learning objectives

  • Compare vectorized and event-driven backtests and state the strengths of each.
  • Describe the event types and their order in an event-driven simulator.
  • Detect and remove look-ahead bias in a backtest.

Subtopics

1. Vectorized backtests

A vectorized backtest computes positions and returns for all dates with array operations. It is fast and easy to read, and it is good for exploring ideas. Its weakness is that it is easy to use information from the same bar that the trade depends on.

2. Event-driven simulation

An event-driven simulator processes market data, signals, orders and fills in time order from a queue. Each event sees only the state available at its time. This structure makes execution assumptions explicit and testable.

3. Look-ahead bias

Look-ahead bias occurs when a decision uses a price or a signal that would not have been known when the trade was placed. A signal computed from a bar's close cannot be filled at that close. A realistic fill occurs at the next available price after the signal.

4. Latency and fill models

Orders take time to reach the venue, and fills depend on the book at arrival. A fill model that delays execution by one or more bars, or that uses the book state at arrival, is more realistic than filling at the signal price.

Mathematical theory

Let s_t be a signal computed from data up to the close of bar t, and r_t the return from the close of bar t to the close of bar t plus one. A realistic strategy return is s_t times r_(t plus 1), because the position is taken after the signal and held through the next bar. Using s_t times r_t mixes information from the same bar and overstates performance.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Same-bar versus next-bar returns

Compute strategy returns for a simple alternating signal in two ways: using the same-bar return and using the next-bar return. Compare the totals.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(90)
price = 100 * np.exp(np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.005, 1000)))
signal = (np.arange(1000) % 20 < 10).astype(int)
ret = np.diff(price) / price[:-1]
pos_same_bar = signal[:-1] * ret
pos_next_bar = signal[:-2] * ret[1:]
print(round(pos_same_bar.sum(), 4), round(pos_next_bar.sum(), 4))

Experiment 2: Fill delay parameter

Add a parameter that delays fills by k bars in a simple loop, then report how total return changes as k increases from zero to five.

Book references

  • Chan, Quantitative Trading: How to Build Your Own Algorithmic Trading Business (Wiley, 2nd edition). Read the sections on backtesting.
  • backtrader documentation (backtrader.com). Read the sections on order execution and broker simulation.

Completion criteria

  • Experiment 1 reports both totals, and you explain why the same-bar total is not achievable.
  • Experiment 2 reports the total return for each delay from zero to five bars.
  • Your backtest code has a comment at each point where information becomes available.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Fill models are simplified, and queue position, partial fills and rejections are not modeled in these examples.
  • Vectorized and event-driven results should agree for simple strategies, and disagreement usually signals a bug.

Learning objectives

  • Include commissions, fees and slippage in a backtest and report results net of costs.
  • Explain how survivorship bias and selection bias inflate backtest results.
  • Assess how strategy turnover changes sensitivity to cost assumptions.

Subtopics

1. Commissions and fees

Commissions, exchange fees and clearing fees are charged per trade or per contract. For high-turnover strategies, these charges can exceed the gross return. Fee schedules change, so the assumed values should be recorded with each backtest.

2. Slippage

Slippage is the difference between the expected fill price and the actual fill price. It depends on order size, volatility and liquidity. A flat slippage assumption is a simplification that is acceptable only when orders are small relative to volume.

3. Survivorship and selection bias

Testing only on instruments that still exist today removes failures and overstates returns. Selection bias occurs when strategies are chosen after looking at results on the same data. Both biases must be addressed in the data design, not corrected afterward.

4. Turnover and cost sensitivity

A strategy that trades a large share of its portfolio each day pays costs on every trade. Reporting the Sharpe ratio across several cost levels shows whether the edge survives realistic assumptions.

Mathematical theory

Net return equals gross return minus turnover times the cost rate. Turnover is the fraction of the portfolio traded in a period, and the cost rate is the total cost per unit traded, often expressed in basis points. Breakeven cost is the cost rate at which the net Sharpe ratio falls to zero.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Sharpe ratio across cost levels

Given a synthetic gross return series and a daily turnover series, compute the annualized net Sharpe ratio at cost levels of 0, 5 and 10 basis points.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(100)
gross = rng.normal(0.0004, 0.01, 1000)
turnover = rng.uniform(0.2, 1.0, 1000)
for cost_bps in (0, 5, 10):
    net = gross - turnover * cost_bps / 10000
    sharpe = net.mean() / net.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(252)
    print(cost_bps, round(sharpe, 2))

Experiment 2: Survivorship illustration

Simulate a universe in which some instruments delist with poor returns. Compare the average return of the instruments that survive to the end with the average return of the full universe, and report the gap.

Book references

  • Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu, "Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism" (Notices of the AMS, 2014).
  • Narang, Inside the Black Box (Wiley). Read the sections on transaction costs and their effect on strategies.

Completion criteria

  • Experiment 1 reports the net Sharpe ratio at all three cost levels, and you state the breakeven cost.
  • Experiment 2 reports the survivor-minus-universe return gap.
  • Your backtest report lists every cost and data assumption in one table.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Flat cost rates ignore the rise in impact costs for large orders and during stressed markets.
  • The turnover series here is random, so the example shows the arithmetic of costs and not a real strategy's trading pattern.

Learning objectives

  • Choose one capstone project that combines at least two earlier topics.
  • Write measurable acceptance criteria and weekly milestones.
  • Run an end-to-end smoke test on sample data before adding features.

Subtopics

1. Choosing the scope

Good capstones are narrow enough to finish and broad enough to show judgment. Three options fit this roadmap: a FIX-connected paper trader, a market data pipeline with bar construction and cleaning, or a backtesting engine with costs and validation. Pick one and state what you will leave out.

2. Milestones

Break the project into milestones that each produce something testable, such as a parser, a data loader, a model and a report. A milestone is complete only when its tests pass, so progress is measured by evidence rather than by time spent.

3. Acceptance criteria

Write acceptance criteria before building. Each criterion should state an input, an expected output and a tolerance. Criteria such as the replay test passes on three logs or the cost model matches a hand calculation can be checked without judgment.

4. Documentation

A capstone needs a README that explains how to install, run and test it, plus a short design note that records assumptions. Documentation is part of the deliverable, because a project that no one else can run has limited value.

Mathematical theory

A pipeline is a composition of functions, each mapping inputs to outputs with a defined schema. Testing each function separately and then testing the composition gives strong evidence that the whole system behaves as intended.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Smoke test of a small pipeline

Build a three-step pipeline that drops missing prices, computes returns and removes the first row. Run it on a small sample with a missing value and confirm the output has no gaps.

import pandas as pd
def pipeline(df):
    df = df.dropna()
    df["ret"] = df["price"].pct_change()
    return df.dropna()
sample = pd.DataFrame({"price": [100.0, 101.0, None, 103.0, 102.0]})
print(pipeline(sample))

Experiment 2: Acceptance test list

Write five acceptance tests for your chosen capstone, each with an input, an expected output and a tolerance, and check that each test can fail.

Book references

  • Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly). Read the chapters on data pipelines and reliability.
  • FIX Trading Community (fixtrading.org). Use the protocol documentation from the connectivity week as a reference.

Completion criteria

  • Your milestone document lists five measurable acceptance criteria with tolerances.
  • The smoke test in Experiment 1 runs without error and returns the expected rows.
  • Your scope note names at least two features you deliberately left out.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Scope estimates are often optimistic, so the first milestone should be small enough to finish in a week.
  • Sample data is used for the smoke test, so the pipeline still needs testing on real data under the firm's data rules.

Learning objectives

  • Use a language model API to classify financial sentences into defined labels.
  • Measure agreement between model labels and human labels with standard metrics.
  • Version prompts and record the model identifier used for each run.

Subtopics

1. Classification tasks

Typical tasks include labeling sentences from earnings calls or news as positive, negative or neutral, or tagging statements as hawkish or dovish. Each label set must be defined precisely in writing, because vague categories produce inconsistent labels from people and from models.

2. Structured output

Ask for a fixed set of labels in a fixed format, and parse the response strictly. Free-form answers are hard to score and easy to misread. Reject any response that does not match the expected format, and count those rejections as errors.

3. Evaluation against human labels

Label a sample by hand, run the model on the same items, and compare. Accuracy, precision and recall per class, and Cohen's kappa, which adjusts for chance agreement, are standard measures. Report the sample size along with each figure.

4. Versioning and cost

Store the prompt text, the model identifier, the date and the parameters for each run. Model versions change over time, so a result is reproducible only if these details are recorded. Track token use and latency, because they determine cost at scale.

Mathematical theory

Cohen's kappa equals the observed agreement minus the agreement expected by chance, divided by one minus the expected agreement. A value of one means perfect agreement, and a value of zero means agreement no better than chance.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: One labeled call through the API

Send a single financial sentence to the model with a fixed label set and a low maximum output length, then print the label returned. Use the model identifier current on the Anthropic documentation site.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",
    max_tokens=20,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Label as positive, negative, or neutral. Reply with the label only: Revenue beat expectations."}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text)

Experiment 2: Agreement on a hand-labeled sample

Hand-label 50 sentences, run the same prompt over them, and compute accuracy and Cohen's kappa. Repeat the run to see how much the labels change between calls.

Book references

  • Anthropic API documentation (docs.claude.com). Read the sections on the Messages API and on writing clear prompts.
  • Hugging Face NLP course (huggingface.co/learn/nlp-course). Read the chapter on text classification and its evaluation.

Completion criteria

  • Your agreement report covers 50 labeled sentences and gives accuracy and Cohen's kappa.
  • Your prompt file has a version number, and the run log records the model identifier.
  • You report how many responses failed the format check and how you treated them.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • A sample of 50 sentences gives wide uncertainty, so treat the agreement figure as a rough estimate.
  • Model behavior can change between versions, and results from one version do not carry over automatically to another.

Learning objectives

  • Split documents into chunks and index them for retrieval.
  • Measure retrieval quality with recall at k on labeled queries.
  • Check whether generated answers are supported by the retrieved passages.

Subtopics

1. Chunking

Documents are split into passages small enough to fit a model's context and specific enough to match a query. Chunks that cut a sentence or a table in half lose meaning, so boundaries should follow the document's structure where possible.

2. Indexing and retrieval

Each chunk is turned into a vector, either with term weights such as TF-IDF or with a learned embedding. A query is matched to the nearest chunks by similarity, and the top few are passed to the model as context.

3. Grounding and citation

The answer should cite the passages it used, and a reader should be able to check each claim against them. An answer with no supporting passage is a sign that retrieval failed or that the model went beyond its context.

4. Evaluation

Recall at k measures whether the correct passage appears among the top k results. Faithfulness measures whether each claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved text. Both should be measured on a labeled set of queries before the system is trusted.

Mathematical theory

Cosine similarity between a query vector q and a chunk vector d equals their dot product divided by the product of their norms. Retrieval ranks chunks by this value. Recall at k equals the number of queries whose correct chunk appears in the top k, divided by the number of queries.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Tiny TF-IDF retriever

Index three short documents with TF-IDF, search with a query, and return the index of the best match. Extend the test to 20 queries and report recall at 3.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
import numpy as np
docs = ["Bond duration measures price sensitivity",
        "FIX logon uses heartbeat intervals",
        "Dollar bars sample by traded value"]
queries = ["how sensitive is a bond price to rates"]
vec = TfidfVectorizer().fit(docs)
sims = (vec.transform(queries) @ vec.transform(docs).T).toarray()[0]
print(int(np.argmax(sims)))

Experiment 2: Faithfulness check

For ten generated answers, list each claim and mark whether a retrieved passage supports it. Report the share of supported claims and inspect the unsupported ones.

Book references

  • Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks" (arXiv:2005.11401). Read the method and experiment sections.
  • Hugging Face NLP course (huggingface.co/learn/nlp-course). Read the material on semantic search and embeddings.

Completion criteria

  • Your recall at 3 is reported on 20 labeled queries with the number of hits.
  • Your faithfulness check covers ten answers, with each claim marked supported or unsupported.
  • You document the chunk size and overlap and explain how you chose them.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • TF-IDF matches words rather than meaning, so it misses paraphrases that embeddings would catch.
  • A corpus of three documents is far too small to show how retrieval behaves at production scale.

Learning objectives

  • Solve expected-value puzzles by setting up the right conditional probabilities.
  • Use combinatorics to count outcomes in discrete problems.
  • Check a puzzle answer by simulation before accepting it.

Subtopics

1. Expected-value puzzles

Many interview questions ask for an expected payoff of a game. The method is to list the outcomes, assign probabilities, and sum the weighted payoffs. Linearity of expectation often simplifies the work when the game is a sum of simple events.

2. Conditioning and surprises

Puzzles such as the Monty Hall problem reward careful conditioning. Information about which option was revealed changes the probabilities, and intuition is often wrong. Writing out the full sample space resolves most disputes.

3. Combinatorics

Counting problems use permutations, combinations and symmetry. The key step is deciding whether order matters and whether outcomes are equally likely. Errors usually come from treating unequal outcomes as equal.

4. Verifying by simulation

A quick simulation can check an analytic answer to within a small error. If the two disagree, either the setup or the calculation is wrong, and the discrepancy is a useful signal to revisit the reasoning.

Mathematical theory

The expected value of a payoff X is the sum over outcomes of the payoff times its probability. For a game that pays 10 dollars if two fair coin tosses both land heads and nothing otherwise, the expected payoff is 10 times one quarter, which is 2.50 dollars.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Monty Hall by simulation

Simulate the Monty Hall game for many trials, always switching after the host reveals a goat, and compare the win rate with the analytic answer of two thirds.

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(120)
n = 200_000
car = rng.integers(0, 3, n)
pick = rng.integers(0, 3, n)
host = np.array([next(d for d in range(3) if d != c and d != p) for c, p in zip(car, pick)])
switch = np.array([next(d for d in range(3) if d != h and d != p) for h, p in zip(host, pick)])
print(round((switch == car).mean(), 3))

Experiment 2: Timed practice set

Solve ten expected-value and conditioning puzzles, two minutes each, without notes. Record your answers and whether each was correct after checking.

Book references

  • Zhou, A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews (CreateSpace). Work through the probability section.
  • Blitzstein and Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press). Read the sections on conditional probability.

Completion criteria

  • The simulated switch win rate in Experiment 1 is within 0.01 of two thirds.
  • You solve at least eight of the ten timed puzzles correctly.
  • You explain the Monty Hall result in two sentences that use conditional probability.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • Puzzle sources differ in wording, and some interview questions are ambiguous, so state assumptions before solving.
  • Timed practice measures speed under artificial pressure, which may not reflect how an interviewer evaluates reasoning.

Learning objectives

  • Choose the right Python data structure for a problem and justify the choice with complexity.
  • Implement a priority structure with lazy deletion for cancelled orders.
  • Outline a market data or order system design and state its trade-offs.

Subtopics

1. Data structures and complexity

Heaps give fast access to the best price, dictionaries give constant-time lookup by identifier, and deques support fast insertion at both ends. State the complexity of each operation and explain why it matters for a given workload.

2. Lazy deletion

Removing an arbitrary element from a heap is slow. Lazy deletion marks cancelled entries and skips them when they reach the top. This keeps cancellations cheap, at the cost of some extra memory until the stale entries are removed.

3. System design for market data

A market data system receives feeds, normalizes them, and distributes updates to many consumers with bounded latency. Key questions include ordering, gap detection, fan-out cost and what happens when a consumer falls behind.

4. Communicating trade-offs

Interviewers look for clear reasoning about alternatives. State the options, the criteria, the chosen option and what would change the decision. A clear trade-off discussion often matters more than the final design.

Mathematical theory

A binary heap supports insertion and removal of the top element in logarithmic time, so n operations take order n log n time. Lazy deletion adds a constant cost per cancellation, and the amortized cost of cleaning stale entries remains logarithmic per removal.

Python experiments

Experiment 1: Bid book with lazy cancellation

Implement a bid structure with a heap and a set of cancelled identifiers, add orders, cancel one, and check that the best bid skips the cancelled order.

import heapq
class BidBook:
    def __init__(self):
        self.heap = []
        self.cancelled = set()
    def add(self, price, oid):
        heapq.heappush(self.heap, (-price, oid))
    def cancel(self, oid):
        self.cancelled.add(oid)
    def best(self):
        while self.heap and self.heap[0][1] in self.cancelled:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap)
        return -self.heap[0][0] if self.heap else None
b = BidBook()
b.add(100.0, 1)
b.add(101.5, 2)
b.cancel(2)
print(b.best())

Experiment 2: Design outline

Write a one-page design for a market data fan-out system with a latency budget, a gap-recovery path and a slow-consumer policy, then review it against the four trade-off steps above.

Book references

  • McDowell, Cracking the Coding Interview (CareerCup). Read the chapters on data structures and on system design.
  • Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly). Read the chapters on messaging and stream processing.

Completion criteria

  • Your bid structure returns the correct best bid after the cancellation in Experiment 1, and you add a test for re-adding a cancelled identifier.
  • Your design outline covers the latency budget, gap recovery and slow-consumer policy.
  • You solve ten timed coding problems and record the number solved within the time limit.

Research limitations and assumptions

  • The lazy-deletion example does not handle re-adding a cancelled identifier, which needs a version counter in production.
  • Interview formats vary by firm, so practice should cover several formats rather than one.

fields.name: 12-Week Quant and AI Roadmap
fields.description:
Twelve weeks with five topics a week and one study day per topic at 150 minutes. The track moves from probability and time series to FIX connectivity, market structure, fixed income, machine learning, performance engineering and interview preparation.

Limitation: the study links were not checked against live sites when this fixture was built. Confirm each link before relying on it.

fields.title: Week 1: Probability and statistics foundations
fields.deliverable: A reproducible notebook that simulates normal and Student-t returns, compares tail-loss frequencies, and includes a one-page written summary of the results.

fields.title: Week 2: Time series and stochastic processes
fields.deliverable: A short report comparing an ARIMA model and a GARCH(1,1) model on one index's daily returns, with out-of-sample forecast errors and a cointegration check on one pair.

fields.title: Week 3: Linear algebra and numerical Python
fields.deliverable: A notebook that estimates a covariance matrix for 20 ETFs with and without shrinkage, reports eigenvalue spectra, and benchmarks a vectorized computation against a Python loop.

fields.title: Week 4: FIX protocol and trading connectivity
fields.deliverable: A parser for sample FIX logs, and a client that logs on, sends heartbeats, processes an ExecutionReport and recovers from a sequence gap against a local simulator.

fields.title: Week 5: Market microstructure and order management
fields.deliverable: A script that rebuilds a limit order book from a sample message feed and measures spreads and depth, plus a written pre-trade risk checklist for an order gateway.

fields.title: Week 6: Fixed income and derivatives pricing
fields.deliverable: A notebook that bootstraps a zero curve from par swap rates, prices a 5-year bond, and reports DV01 and convexity alongside a QuantLib cross-check.

fields.title: Week 7: Futures, forex and market data handling
fields.deliverable: A continuous futures series built from raw contract data with documented roll adjustments, plus a cleaning report covering bad ticks and timestamp issues.

fields.title: Week 8: Machine learning fundamentals
fields.deliverable: A reproducible gradient boosting model for next-day direction, trained on time-ordered splits, with a baseline comparison and a calibration report.

fields.title: Week 9: Deep learning and sequence models
fields.deliverable: A PyTorch LSTM that forecasts next-day volatility, trained on a time-ordered validation split with seeded runs and compared against a GARCH baseline.

fields.title: Week 10: Machine learning for finance
fields.deliverable: A triple-barrier labeling pipeline with purged cross-validation, a meta-labeling layer, and a report with deflated Sharpe and overfitting diagnostics.

fields.title: Week 11: Performance engineering and backtesting
fields.deliverable: A profiled backtest with a Numba-accelerated hot loop, equivalence tests against the original code, and a realism checklist covering costs, latency and survivorship.

fields.title: Week 12: Capstone, LLMs for financial text, and interview preparation
fields.deliverable: A capstone milestone that combines FIX connectivity or a data pipeline with a tested model, an LLM text-classification evaluation, and a log of interview practice sessions.
